# Draft:Battle of the Strait of Hormuz (2026)

1
The Battle of the Strait of Hormuz is described as an ongoing multi-domain military engagement that began in March 2026. It is fought primarily between the armed forces of the United States and the Islamic Republic of Iran, and centers on control of the Strait of Hormuz, a 24-mile-wide maritime chokepoint. According to reports, the conflict began after Iranian forces effectively closed the waterway following coordinated U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iranian leadership. The United States then launched a multistage operation aimed at degrading Iranian asymmetric naval and aerial capabilities and reopening the strait to international commercial shipping.
Strategic background
Tensions escalated on 28 February 2026, when the United States and Israel reportedly carried out Operation Epic Fury, a series of coordinated airstrikes targeting Iranian military facilities, nuclear sites, and leadership. According to these reports, the strikes resulted in the death of Iran's Supreme Leader, Ali Khamenei.
In response, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) reportedly transmitted warnings to maritime traffic and effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian forces are said to have begun attacks on commercial shipping using airborne drones, projectiles, and unmanned explosive boats. Such attacks were reported across the strait, the Persian Gulf, and the Gulf of Oman. Following reports that Iran had begun planting naval mines in the waterway, U.S. President Donald Trump demanded their removal. The United States subsequently began a military campaign intended to degrade Iran's area-denial capabilities.
Order of battle
United States and allied forces
The stated U.S. objective was to reduce the threat posed by Iranian mines, armed boats, and cruise missiles to a level that would permit the safe escort of commercial vessels. According to statements attributed to Air Force General Dan Caine, the operation involved a repurposed aerial strike force.
* Strike aircraft: The United States Air Force reportedly repurposed A-10 Thunderbolt II attack aircraft for maritime strike missions. Equipped with titanium-lined cockpits, nose-mounted 30 mm cannons, and wing-mounted bombs, the aircraft were tasked with targeting fast-attack watercraft along the southern flank of the strait.
* Attack helicopters: Apache helicopters operated by the United States Army were reportedly deployed to target Iranian mine-laying boats using AGM-114 Hellfire missiles. Apache helicopters from unnamed allied states were also reported to have participated in intercepting one-way attack drones.
* Fighter aircraft: Other fighter aircraft already stationed in the region were reportedly used against small attack boats and missile threats.
* Ground and amphibious forces: The United States Department of Defense reportedly deployed roughly 2,200 U.S. Marines, including elements of the 31st Marine Expeditionary Unit, to the Middle East. Their potential mission set reportedly included securing the strait or seizing fortified islands off Iran's southern coast.
* Allied naval assets: The French Navy reportedly pledged to send a dozen ships to the broader Middle East, including two frigates assigned to escort missions.
A capability gap reportedly existed at the outset of the campaign because U.S. littoral combat ships used for mine-clearing had recently been moved out of the region.
Islamic Republic of Iran
Defense of the strait was reportedly overseen jointly by the IRGC and the Iranian Navy. Iranian strategy was described as relying heavily on asymmetric warfare, using large numbers of expendable and concealable assets.
* Naval assets: Iran reportedly deployed fleets of small fast-attack boats and unmanned surface vessels carrying explosive charges. Additional boats were reportedly kept in reserve in coastal tunnels and concealed island facilities.
* Aerial and missile assets: The IRGC reportedly operated fortified land-based cruise missile batteries and airborne drones, including mobile cruise missile systems mounted on trucks.
* Naval mines: Iranian forces were reported to possess a large stockpile of naval mines, including variants anchored to the sea floor and capable of remote detonation as target vessels passed overhead.
Course of the battle
Early naval clashes and mining operations
As commercial shipping halted, Iranian forces reportedly began direct denial operations in the waterway. U.S. military intelligence reportedly determined that Iranian minelayers had begun seeding the strait with naval mines. In response, the U.S. military reportedly tracked and destroyed 16 Iranian mine-laying vessels.
Iranian drone boats and fast-attack craft also reportedly targeted commercial shipping. Among the reported incidents, the MKD VYOM was said to have been struck by a drone boat, causing an engine-room explosion. A separate drone strike reportedly hit the tanker Sonangol Namibe near Kuwait, more than 500 miles from the strait.
U.S. air-to-sea campaign
To establish control over the waterway, the United States reportedly began an air campaign against IRGC bases and cruise missile batteries along the Iranian coastline.
Within the strait itself, low-flying A-10 aircraft and Apache helicopters reportedly engaged Iranian fast-attack boats in repeated clashes. According to U.S. statements, these operations targeted vessels attempting to harass shipping in the area. By 19 March, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth reportedly stated that U.S. strikes and engagements had damaged or destroyed more than 120 Iranian naval vessels.
Tactical challenges and geography
The geography of the combat zone was widely described as a major factor in the pace and character of the battle. At its narrowest point, the Strait of Hormuz is approximately 24 miles wide, keeping U.S. and allied vessels within range of Iranian shore-based defenses. Analyst Michael Connell was cited as arguing that the confined waters enabled Iranian cruise missiles fired from deep inland to threaten ships in the strait.
Despite reported losses to Iranian naval forces, analysts including Farzin Nadimi argued that Iran's coastal tunnel systems would allow a significant portion of its assets to survive sustained bombing. U.S. officials reportedly estimated that weeks of continuous combat operations would be required to reduce Iranian capabilities sufficiently to permit safer maritime transit. Even if commercial passage resumed, analysts warned that vessels could remain vulnerable to missile strikes from surviving Iranian batteries.
